newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Commerzbank chairman new target in tax probe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Commerzbank chairman new target in tax probe.

text.p: German prosecutors on Monday said they had extended a probe into alleged corporate tax evasion at Commerzbank to the bank's management board chairman Martin Kohlhaussen, reflecting Bonn's mounting determination to rein in lost fiscal revenues.

Kohlhaussen, a high-profile executive who has complained repeatedly about over-aggressive raids by tax investigators on bank premises and records, is being linked with several balance sheet items, including allegedly inaccurate calculations of bank reserves.
"We are at the very beginning of these investigations. It is too early to say when we will have a result," said public prosecutors' spokesman Job Tilmann in a telephone interview.

The Kohlhaussen probe is part of a seven-month-old investigation into Commerzbank, Germany's third largest bank, which was forced earlier this year to repay several hundred millions of marks in back-tax for the period from 1984 to 1995.

Commerzbank, which is contesting the size of the repayment, citing "differences of opinion" with tax authorities, said Kohlhaussen's involvement had come about because he signed tax returns during the period.

"It has to be made very clear that these allegations are not accusations of personal wrongdoing. They only concern the bank's own tax returns," said Commerzbank spokesman Peter Pietsch in a telephone interview.
Three other Commerzbank staff, whose names and rank have not been revealed, are also being investigated.

Tilmann said legal constraints banned him from giving precise details on the probe but said there were "fairly clear" indications that Commerzbank had booked losses at group level for U.S. subsidiaries which had been already written off in the U.S. and subsequently overstated its allocation to reserves.
The move by investigators reflects the cash-strapped German government's mounting determination to clamp down on tax evasion, with annual losses due to tax fraudsters estimated at billions of marks.

The probe is running parallel to the two-year-old investigation into allegations that staff at Commerzbank and other major banks abetted tax evasion by clients by helping them shift funds to hard-to-trace accounts in Luxembourg.
Der Spiegel magazine on Monday said as many as 17,000 Germans are currently being investigated for tax evasion.

The probe, which has involved hundreds of raids on bank branches, followed the exodus of billions of marks to Luxembourg and other tax havens after Germany slapped a 30 percent withholding tax on interest income in 1994.
Moving funds abroad to avoid that tax is not illegal, but failing to report interest income to fiscal authorities in Germany is in breach of the law.

Senior German bank executives including Kohlhaussen have complained loudly that investigators were panicking customers who had opened accounts in Luxembourg in good faith and were also violating bank secrecy codes.

Commerzbank on Monday repeated its determination to challenge the charges of corporate tax evasion. Spokesman Peter Pietsch said the bank had paid 5.2 billion marks ($3.49 billion) in tax during the period in question -- "a not inconsiderable sum".
He also recalled Kohlhaussen's own expressions of anger earlier this year at a raid on the Commerzbank premises in Frankfurt in February. The move, Kohlhaussen said, was "totally out of proportion."
It was unclear what penalty Kohlhaussen might face if found guilty on the corporate tax charges. Tilmann said the maximum penalty for tax evasion was a five-year prison term.
